clue.text: Attractive German without pants

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish or no good, and letters that have gone to the bad no longer sit where they were put

parts.note: thirteen letters, exactly the thirteen the answer needs, in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like a deletion instruction and is really just more fodder — the whole two words go into the mix, which is why nothing has to be taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive -> MOUTH-WATERING: food that makes you salivate is irresistible, and the word has widened to anything tempting, an offer or a prospect.

clue.text: Army man reformed country

indicators.note: to re-form something is to shape it again, so the letters are made up a second time

parts.note: the seven letters of the soldier, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a soldier who has mended his ways; the country was itself renamed, which makes 'reformed' do double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: country -> MYANMAR: the south-east Asian state formerly called Burma, so the bare word 'country' points at it as one nation among many.

clue.text: Using leverage to infiltrate American rebellions

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to slip inside an organisation unnoticed, so this piece goes within the other rather than beside it

parts.note: US is the everyday short form of American, and it splits either side of what enters it
to prise a lid is to lever it, so prising is using leverage

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like political meddling abroad, which is exactly the sense the setter wants you stuck on while two letters are being pushed apart.
explanation.definitionFit: rebellions -> UPRISINGS: an uprising is a popular revolt against those in power, so the plural is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Personal issue with dog breed? No, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection shows you a thing the wrong way round, so the assembled letters are read from the far end

parts.note: the pug is a small flat-faced breed
nah is the spoken form of no

explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' reads as a change of mind in the surface and as a mirror in the wordplay, and the enumeration 4-2 tells you the answer is hyphenated.
explanation.definitionFit: Personal issue -> HANG-UP: a hang-up is an inhibition someone cannot get past, the private neurosis sense rather than a phone call.

clue.text: Article on parishioner taxes is in opposition

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing sits on another by resting above it, so the article goes at the top

parts.note: AN is the indefinite article, the one used before a vowel
a tithe was the tenth of his produce a parishioner owed the church
the little verb is taken at face value and joins the end

explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'is' looks like joinery holding the sentence together and is really two of the letters, which is the trick worth remembering here.
explanation.definitionFit: opposition -> ANTITHESIS: in rhetoric an antithesis is the exact contrary set against a thing, naming opposition as a noun.

clue.text: Fish caught and inspected

indicators.note: to catch what somebody says is to hear it, so the sound of the word is wanted and not its spelling

parts.note: the ide is a European freshwater fish, and its name said aloud is spelt this way

explanation.walkthrough: Anglers' fish names are a small vocabulary worth collecting — ide, dace, chub, ling — because setters reach for them whenever a short odd-sounding word is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: inspected -> EYED: to eye something is to look it over deliberately, so the past tense is a plain synonym for having inspected it.

clue.text: I snooze in church if circumstances require it

parts.note: the pronoun is taken as the single letter it looks like
a nap is a short snooze
this one is written down exactly as it stands
CH is the standard map abbreviation for church

explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces and not an indicator among them: when a clue gives you no instruction words at all, it is telling you the parts simply follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: if circumstances require it -> IN A PINCH: the idiom means at need, when nothing better is to hand, so the whole phrase answers the whole phrase.

clue.text: Pleased at cheque finally clearing

parts.note: glad and pleased are the same everyday feeling

indicators.note: what happens finally happens at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is taken

parts.note: the last letter of cheque

explanation.walkthrough: A cheque clearing is banking; a clearing in a wood is forestry. The whole surface leans on that one word doing two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: clearing -> GLADE: a glade is an open grassy space among trees, which is exactly what foresters and walkers call a clearing.

clue.text: Agreement about supporting educational establishments

indicators.note: whatever supports a thing lies underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means further down the column

parts.note: unis is the familiar short form of universities
a book on birds is a book about birds

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads bottom-up: the piece named first ends up last, because supporting something means sitting beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreement -> UNISON: voices in unison sing one note together, and the word carried over to any complete accord between people.

clue.text: Rapper regularly performing somewhere on stage

indicators.note: doing something regularly means doing it at even intervals, so every second letter is taken and the rest left

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of rApPeR
a show that is performing is on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rapper regularly performing' paints a gig, and every word of it is machinery: a letter count, and the theatre sense of ON.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere on stage -> APRON: the apron is the strip of stage jutting out in front of the curtain, so the phrase names a place rather than a garment.

clue.text: On the other hand, the horse is not tailless

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, and a creature without one has lost exactly that much

parts.note: the article is written down as it stands
a nag is a worn-out horse
is not contracts to AIN'T, which loses its tail

explanation.walkthrough: 'the horse is not tailless' is a sentence about a horse's tail and an instruction about a word's, and the joke is that the horse keeps its tail while AIN'T does not.
explanation.definitionFit: On the other hand -> THEN AGAIN: both are set phrases used to introduce a contrary thought, so one whole idiom swaps for the other.

clue.text: Disease vector medical officers leave out at first

parts.note: a medical officer is an MO, and more than one are MOs
to quit a job is to leave it

indicators.note: what comes at first comes before everything else, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of out

explanation.walkthrough: A vector is not a direction here but the creature that carries a disease between hosts, which is the piece of biology the definition is banking on.
explanation.definitionFit: Disease vector -> MOSQUITO: the mosquito carries malaria and dengue from person to person, and is the textbook example of a vector species.

clue.text: Guns from American's murder case in Paris found near Belgium

indicators.note: a case is the shell a thing sits in, so what is wanted is the pair of letters at the outside

parts.note: B is Belgium's international vehicle registration letter
to ice someone is American slang for killing them

indicators.note: being near something means standing beside it, so this letter joins the rest end-on rather than going inside them

parts.note: the outer letters of Paris

explanation.walkthrough: A murder case in Paris is a news story, and not one word of it means what it says: the city contributes only its shell, and the country only its number plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Guns -> BICEPS: gym slang calls well-developed upper arms guns, so the definition is a colloquial nickname for the muscle rather than a weapon.

clue.text: Dreadful tour spoiled by this group's singer

indicators.note: food that has spoiled has gone off, and letters that go off end up somewhere other than where they were

parts.note: dreadful here means simply bad
the tour goes in whole, four more letters for the mix
someone inside a group calls it ours, so this group's is OUR

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful tour spoiled' reads as one complaint about a band, and only the first word is a synonym while the third is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: singer -> TROUBADOUR: a troubadour was a medieval poet who performed his own love songs, so 'singer' names the wider class he belongs to.

clue.text: Musical in two parts?

definitions.meaning: Jonathan Larson's Broadway show about young artists who cannot pay their landlord
the past participle of rend: a torn garment has been split in two

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters, no indicators and a question mark: that shape almost always means the clue splits in two and each half defines the answer on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses at once: the Broadway musical of that name, and the past participle of rend, which is what a thing torn down the middle is.

clue.text: Staggering, Herculean power fills legendary Irish figure

indicators.note: someone staggering cannot hold a straight line, and these letters do not hold their line either
what fills a space is spread right through it, so the odd letter lands among the others instead of at an end

parts.note: all nine letters go into the mix
P is the physicist's symbol for power, and the tenth letter needed

explanation.walkthrough: Herculean strength and Irish legend belong to two different mythologies, which is what makes the surface sound like one sentence when it is really a heap of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: legendary Irish figure -> LEPRECHAUN: the leprechaun is the shoemaker fairy of Irish folklore, guarding his crock of gold — a figure of legend rather than history.

clue.text: Parcels in transit to Long Ashton getting redirected

indicators.note: what is in something lies inside it, so the letters sit within the words that follow instead of being spelt out
traffic that is redirected is sent the other way, and these letters run the other way too

parts.note: run the words together and this nine-letter string spans them, from the end of transit to the start of Ashton

explanation.walkthrough: Long Ashton is a real village outside Bristol, and naming somewhere plausible is how a setter stops you reading the words as a string of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Parcels -> AGNOLOTTI: agnolotti are squares of pasta folded around a filling, and parcels is the standard menu word for that shape.

clue.text: Underground hub's very graphic stripping

indicators.note: to strip a thing is to take its covering off, and a word's covering is the letter at each end

parts.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
graphic means PICTORIAL, which is stripped of its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'very graphic stripping' is written to sound like something a censor would object to, and the only thing being undressed is a nine-letter adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Underground hub -> VICTORIA: Victoria is one of the busiest interchanges on the London Underground, so the generic phrase points at a named station.

clue.text: Shady assassins essentially promising to eliminate leader

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is what lies at its heart, so the letter at the exact centre is wanted
the leader of a word is the letter at its head, and this says to get rid of it

parts.note: assassins runs to nine letters, and the fifth sits at the dead centre
promising means AUSPICIOUS, which gives up the A at its head

explanation.walkthrough: Assassins who are essentially promising is a joke on hitmen with prospects, and the two long words are near-twins: one loses a head, the other lends a heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Shady -> SUSPICIOUS: shady describes a person or deal that invites distrust, matching the sense of arousing suspicion rather than feeling it.

clue.text: Illegible handwriting beginning from squiggly stroke

indicators.note: a word begins with one letter only, and that is the letter this asks you to take

parts.note: the first letter of squiggly
the crawl is the fastest swimming stroke

explanation.walkthrough: 'stroke' is a pen stroke in the surface and a swimming stroke in the wordplay, and swimming strokes — crawl, fly, back — are worth keeping in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Illegible handwriting -> SCRAWL: a scrawl is writing dashed off so carelessly that nobody can read it, so the noun names the unreadable result.

clue.text: I've got the same kitchenware on the counter

indicators.note: to counter a move is to go against it, so these letters run against the direction the clue gives them

parts.note: pans are the kitchenware, and they are what gets turned round

explanation.walkthrough: A kitchen counter is where pans sit, which is why 'on the counter' reads as furniture and works as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: I've got the same -> SNAP: in the card game you call 'Snap!' the moment your card matches, and it became everyday slang for 'me too'.

clue.text: Plain couple that is broken up by Romeo

indicators.note: something broken up has been forced apart, so the newcomer lands inside the pair and splits it

parts.note: a couple is a pair
i.e. is the Latin id est, which translates as that is
Romeo is R in the radio alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Romeo breaking up a couple is Shakespeare on the surface; in the wordplay he is one letter from the NATO spelling alphabet, a set worth learning whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain -> PRAIRIE: a prairie is the flat open grassland of North America, and 'plain' is the general noun for that country — the noun, not the adjective.

clue.text: Has Met dealt with one dividing capital between banks?

indicators.note: cards are dealt out in a fresh order every hand, and these six letters are handed out again the same way

parts.note: the six letters of Has Met, redealt

explanation.walkthrough: The Met dealing with a case is police business, and 'banks' is the pun that has to fall the other way: not the ones holding money but the ones holding water.
explanation.definitionFit: one dividing capital between banks -> THAMES: the river runs through London and separates the city into north and south sides.

clue.text: Spin doctor who lost California court case, ultimately

indicators.note: what happens ultimately happens at the very end, so each word gives up only the letter it closes with

parts.words: doctor who lost California court case
parts.note: the closing letters of the six words in turn: doctoR, whO, losT, CaliforniA, courT, casE

explanation.walkthrough: A spin doctor losing in a California court is a whole news story, and none of it matters except the letter each word ends on — six words, six letters, in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Spin -> ROTATE: to rotate is to turn about an axis, which is the plain physical sense of spin rather than the public-relations one.

clue.text: Bears? Definitely!

definitions.meaning: to carry a load, as in 'tote a bag', is the verb meant; here it takes the third-person -s
clipped teen slang for totally, used to agree with something wholeheartedly

explanation.walkthrough: Two registers a century apart: a word from tote bags and gun-toting, and a word from text messages. The question mark warns you the first reading is the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: Bears -> TOTES as in carrying a load, the sense behind 'tote bag'; and 'totes' is modern slang shortened from totally, meaning absolutely.

clue.text: God can set about creating a heaven

indicators.note: to set a thing about is to turn it round, so the assembly is read from its far end backwards

parts.note: Allah is God in Islam
the can is American for the lavatory, the lav

explanation.walkthrough: Three religions in eight letters: an Islamic name and a slang toilet, turned round to make a Norse afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: a heaven -> VALHALLA: in Norse myth Valhalla is Odin's hall where warriors killed in battle feast for ever, so it serves as a paradise, not the Christian one.

clue.text: Head to lounge

definitions.meaning: Cockney rhyming slang for head shortens a two-word phrase ending in 'bread', since bread rhymes with head
to idle the day away, doing nothing much, is the verb meant here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head to' reads as an instruction to go somewhere, which hides the split: the clue is two definitions with a word of joinery between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Head -> LOAF through the rhyming slang loaf of bread; and to loaf is to lounge about doing nothing, the verb sense.

clue.text: French defeat almost stopped by wingers in pro team sport

indicators.note: almost there means you stop just short, so the last letter never gets written down
a winger plays out on the flank, so the letters wanted are the ones at either edge

parts.note: Napoleon's defeat was Waterloo, one letter short of the whole

indicators.note: whatever stops you gets in your way, so this piece lands in the middle of the other

parts.note: the outer letters of pro

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is football — wingers, a pro team — and the sport is played in a pool. Waterloo is the setter's favourite French defeat because of what its first five letters spell.
explanation.definitionFit: team sport -> WATER POLO: water polo is played seven a side in a swimming pool, so it belongs to the class of team games rather than individual ones.

clue.text: Roadworthiness test for defaced car

indicators.note: to deface a thing is to take its face off, and a word wears its face at the front

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British vehicles
for loses its first letter, its face, and OR is left

explanation.walkthrough: An MOT on a defaced car is a plausible garage scene, and 'for' is the word you have to stop reading as joinery before the clue comes apart.
explanation.definitionFit: car -> MOTOR: motor is the everyday British word for a car, still ordinary in speech long after the full motor car went out of use.

clue.text: County newscast affords hi-res screens

indicators.note: a screen is put up to keep something out of sight, so these words are hiding what sits inside them

parts.note: run the three words together and the county spans them, from the end of newscast to the middle of hi-res

explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters is a long thing to hide, so the setter needs a surface that will carry three unusual words in a row — high-definition television does the job.
explanation.definitionFit: County -> STAFFORDSHIRE: Staffordshire is one of the English shire counties, so the bare word names the class this place belongs to.
